seo.title: Israel-Palestine Conflict 2026: Escalation Risk Map
seo.description: Intelligence report mapping Israel-Palestine escalation risks in 2026 — Gaza ceasefire violations, West Bank settlements, and Lebanon flashpoints.

title: Israel-Palestine Conflict: 2026 Escalation Risk Map
excerpt: The Gaza ceasefire has held in name only, with thousands of violations recorded, Hamas disarmament stalled, and Lebanon flaring repeatedly. This report maps the Israel-Palestine conflict's fault lines and where escalation is most likely next.
content:
Israel-Palestine Conflict: 2026 Escalation Risk Map

A ceasefire that gets violated more than three thousand times is not, in any meaningful sense, a ceasefire. It is a label attached to a war that has changed its rhythm without changing its character. Eight months after President Donald Trump stood beside regional leaders in Sharm el-Sheikh and declared an end to the Gaza war, the territory remains divided, bombed, and starving in slow motion, while the diplomatic architecture built to end the conflict — the Board of Peace, the twenty-point plan, the promised Palestinian technocratic committee — sits largely unimplemented on paper while the killing continues at a reduced but very real pace on the ground.

This is the uncomfortable truth at the center of the Israel-Palestine conflict in mid-2026: the war did not end in October 2025. It downshifted. And downshifted wars carry their own distinct danger, because they create the appearance of resolution — diplomatic credit claimed, headlines moved on, international attention redirected toward Iran, toward Ukraine, toward the South China Sea — while the underlying drivers of escalation remain almost entirely intact. Hamas has not disarmed. Israel has not withdrawn. The West Bank has absorbed the largest single wave of settlement approvals in its modern history. And Lebanon, drawn into the wider regional conflagration through Hezbollah's parallel confrontation with Israel, has cycled through ceasefire announcements with a frequency that itself signals how fragile every one of them actually is.

Executive Summary

The October 2025 Gaza ceasefire, brokered by the Trump administration alongside Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey, ended the most intense phase of direct large-scale combat in Gaza and secured the release of all living Israeli hostages in exchange for thousands of Palestinian prisoners. It did not end the war in any functional sense. By June 2026, Gaza's Government Media Office had documented more than 3,200 Israeli ceasefire violations, with continued Israeli strikes killing close to 1,000 Palestinians since the truce nominally took effect, while humanitarian aid deliveries have consistently fallen far short of the agreement's stipulated volumes.

The structural reason the ceasefire has not produced genuine peace is straightforward: the agreement's second phase, covering Hamas's disarmament, the establishment of a technocratic Palestinian governing committee, and a broader Israeli withdrawal, has stalled almost completely. Israel has conditioned further withdrawal on Hamas disarmament that Hamas has refused to undertake on terms it considers a one-sided demand, while Israeli forces have expanded control well beyond the originally agreed "yellow line" demarcation, now holding more than half of Gaza's territory and threatening, according to the ceasefire's own international overseer, to render the strip permanently divided.

Beyond Gaza, the conflict's geography has widened rather than narrowed. The West Bank has seen its most extensive single wave of Israeli settlement approvals on record, alongside escalating settler violence against Palestinian communities. Lebanon has been drawn into a parallel, repeatedly renegotiated ceasefire with Hezbollah, itself entangled with the broader regional fallout from the 2026 US-Israel war with Iran. Each of these fronts carries its own distinct escalation risk, and each is connected to the others through shared actors, shared grievances, and a shared diplomatic architecture that has proven far better at producing announcements than at producing enforcement.

This report maps the conflict's current fault lines across Gaza, the West Bank, and Lebanon, assesses the strategic logic driving each of the principal actors, and identifies where the risk of renewed large-scale escalation is most acute heading into the second half of 2026.

Background

The current phase of the conflict traces its origin to the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, which killed approximately 1,200 people and saw roughly 250 taken hostage into Gaza. Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza, conducted over the following two years, produced a death toll that by mid-2026 the Gaza Health Ministry placed at over 72,000 confirmed Palestinian deaths, including more than 20,000 children, alongside the near-total destruction of Gaza's housing stock, civilian infrastructure, and healthcare system. The campaign drew sustained international condemnation, including from United Nations bodies and a significant share of the international legal community, even as the United States maintained substantial military and diplomatic support for Israel throughout.

The path to the October 2025 ceasefire ran through more than a year of failed negotiation efforts, mediated variously by Qatar, Egypt, and the United States, each producing temporary pauses that subsequently collapsed back into renewed fighting. The breakthrough came through the Trump administration's twenty-point plan, formally titled "Implementation Steps for President Trump's Proposal for a Comprehensive End of Gaza War," signed by Israel and Hamas in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, on October 9, 2025. Trump announced on October 8 that Israel and Hamas had reached agreement to begin the first phase of the deal, under which all living hostages were to be released in exchange for 2,000 Palestinian prisoners, including 250 serving life sentences, within seventy-two hours of an Israeli withdrawal to pre-designated lines within Gaza.

:antCitation[]{citations="0898e520-9abc-4d59-b43e-7b4fa94d1642" injected="space"}

The ceasefire's signing ceremony itself illustrated the fragility built into the process from the outset. Following mediation by Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey, representatives from roughly thirty countries gathered on October 13 for a signing ceremony led by President Trump, though Israel and Hamas themselves were notably absent, raising early doubts about the summit's ability to achieve tangible progress on the war's core unresolved issues. :antCitation[]{citations="f31b2000-b402-40d9-b8ed-e9531243639b" injected="space"} The ceasefire formally took effect on October 10, 2025, with the first phase's core hostage-prisoner exchange completed within days. On October 13, Hamas released all twenty remaining living Israeli captives in exchange for 250 Palestinians serving long prison sentences and 1,700 Palestinians who had been detained by Israel since October 7, 2023.

:antCitation[]{citations="5bd7e764-0adc-4356-b0e6-1bfa96975c05" injected="space"}

Phase two, intended to move the process from a basic cessation of hostilities toward demilitarization, technocratic governance, and reconstruction, did not begin until January 2026, three months after the initial ceasefire, and has stalled almost entirely since. Six months after the ceasefire's announcement, the twenty-point peace plan had largely stalled on all its promises beyond the initial pause in fighting, the hostage exchange, and a surge in humanitarian aid, with the agreement's remaining seven key pillars showing minimal substantive progress.

:antCitation[]{citations="d398c082-7956-40bb-9553-f3cc6907173d" injected="space"}

Current Situation

The most immediate measure of the ceasefire's dysfunction is the sheer scale of recorded violations. Israel violated the ceasefire agreement at least 3,201 times between October 10, 2025, and June 9, 2026, through continued air, artillery, and direct-fire attacks, according to Gaza's Government Media Office, with confirmed Palestinian deaths in Gaza since October 7, 2023, reaching at least 72,991, including 20,179 children, as of June 10, 2026. :antCitation[]{citations="45faab35-4698-4cf9-aa75-f5b9a74d44d2" injected="space"} The pattern of violence has remained near-constant rather than episodic. An Al Jazeera analysis found Israel had attacked Gaza on 218 of the first 243 days of the ceasefire, meaning only 25 days passed without violent attacks, deaths, or injuries being reported.

:antCitation[]{citations="40daace3-a1ae-4959-98c7-6c26090e047f" injected="space"}

Humanitarian conditions have improved from the war's most acute phase but remain severe. While the ceasefire called for 600 aid trucks to enter Gaza daily, actual deliveries fell far short of that target, and six months into the agreement, 77 percent of Gaza's population still faced acute food insecurity, with severe shortages in medical supplies, fuel, and shelter materials persisting largely due to Israeli restrictions on items classified as "dual-use." :antCitation[]{citations="a631c690-04ac-43f9-8a62-ff6efcc3b09a" injected="space"} Medical evacuation has been similarly constrained. More than 18,000 patients, including 11,000 cancer patients, have required urgent medical treatment but have been unable to evacuate Gaza, with fewer than 400 patients permitted to leave through the Rafah crossing since it reopened in February 2026.

:antCitation[]{citations="d46e51cf-71d9-45ec-936b-8dfbf4524078" injected="space"}

The disarmament impasse sits at the center of the ceasefire's failure to progress. Nikolay Mladenov, director-general of the Gaza Board of Peace overseeing implementation of the US-brokered deal, has warned that a prolonged stalemate risks cementing Gaza's permanent territorial division, leaving two million Palestinians without a viable future while entrenching Israel's long-term presence across more than half of the shattered territory. :antCitation[]{citations="b744808c-3759-44ed-9317-81cda38895fa" injected="space"} Israel's position has been unambiguous on the precondition for further withdrawal. Israeli officials have stated the plan requires Hamas to step back from governing Gaza and have its weapons decommissioned, with Mladenov noting that armed factions maintaining independent military command and control structures cannot be permitted to continue, even as the plan includes provisions for voluntary weapons buyback, conditional amnesty, and safe passage abroad for those willing to disarm. :antCitation[]{citations="d45897bb-3571-4afa-a8c5-6c2d054b3637" injected="space"} Hamas has rejected this framing entirely. A Hamas spokesperson described Israel's disarmament demand as unacceptable and a "crude" double standard that asked concessions only from the Palestinian side, while accusing Mladenov of bias toward Israel and insisting Hamas would not discuss the plan's second phase unless Israel first fully implemented the first phase's terms.

:antCitation[]{citations="7b021af0-1660-40e7-ae73-7e07f4cdba43" injected="space"}

Territorial control on the ground has continued shifting in Israel's favor throughout this impasse. Under the October 2025 agreement, Israeli forces withdrew to a demarcation line known as the "yellow line," which originally encompassed roughly 53 percent of Gaza, but that line has continued shifting toward the Mediterranean Sea, compressing Gaza's displaced population into an ever-shrinking strip of territory. :antCitation[]{citations="5be1baa1-c857-48ea-ab0f-b309b08ce360" injected="space"} A May 2026 Israeli security source signaled the disarmament impasse could trigger a formal resumption of full-scale combat rather than merely continued attrition. An Israeli security source indicated that if Hamas continues refusing to disarm, the Israeli military will restart fighting in Gaza to "complete their mission."

:antCitation[]{citations="320db247-2a3c-42ba-8094-21872ee32923" injected="space"}

The West Bank has simultaneously experienced its own distinct, and in some respects more structurally consequential, escalation. In March 2026, Israel's Cabinet approved 34 settlements across Area C, described as the most extensive such approval in a single Cabinet decision to date, occurring against a backdrop of increasingly frequent and severe settler attacks on Palestinian communities. :antCitation[]{citations="56099f35-0ff2-47ff-8de8-646609eadd65" injected="space"} This wave of settlement expansion carries particular weight because Area C constitutes the portion of the West Bank under full Israeli civil and security control, and its accelerated settlement makes any eventual two-state territorial configuration progressively less geographically viable, independent of whatever happens in Gaza specifically.

Lebanon represents the conflict's third, increasingly volatile front, entangled with both the Gaza ceasefire's fragility and the broader regional fallout from the 2026 US-Israel confrontation with Iran. Following weeks of escalating violence between Israel and Hezbollah that intensified after regional tensions linked to the Iran war, Israel and Lebanon opened direct negotiations during 2026 — the first such direct talks since the failure of the 1983 May 17 Agreement — eventually reaching a ceasefire that took effect April 16, 2026, calling for an initial ten-day cessation of hostilities to enable negotiation toward a permanent agreement, with Lebanon committing to prevent Hezbollah and other non-state armed groups from carrying out attacks against Israel.

:antCitation[]{citations="bc0ebf31-1a35-46f3-9696-4d979fc6bc2e" injected="space"}

That ceasefire has proven no more durable than its Gaza counterpart. The truce was extended multiple times through April and May, with Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem stating the group would not revert to its pre-March posture and would respond to Israeli attacks, before Israel and Hezbollah reached a renewed ceasefire on June 1 under a US proposal, only for Hezbollah to reject the specific terms announced on June 3 and demand instead a comprehensive truce paired with full Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory, with a further US-Qatar-Iran mediated truce reported on June 19. :antCitation[]{citations="edf0a5e9-5b97-4ffa-b835-6d71e82021b1" injected="space"} The repeated cycle of announcement, rejection, and renegotiation across barely two months illustrates just how unstable this front remains, even as it draws comparatively less sustained international attention than Gaza.

Strategic Analysis

The Gaza ceasefire's core structural flaw is that it asked two parties with fundamentally incompatible theories of victory to operate under a shared label of "peace" without resolving which theory would actually govern the territory's future. Israel's strategic objective, consistently articulated by its government throughout this period, is the complete dismantling of Hamas as a military and governing force in Gaza, paired with a security architecture that prevents any future repeat of the October 7 attack. Hamas's strategic objective is survival as a political and military actor with continued relevance in Gaza's governance, paired with the preservation of enough armed capability to maintain leverage in any eventual settlement. These objectives are not merely difficult to reconcile; they are, in their current form, mutually exclusive, which is precisely why the ceasefire's first phase — hostages for prisoners, an initial troop pullback — proved achievable while its second phase — disarmament, governance transition, full withdrawal — has not.

Israel's continued territorial expansion beyond the originally agreed yellow line during this impasse reflects a calculated strategic logic rather than simple drift: each additional kilometer of territory held under Israeli control becomes a fact on the ground that strengthens Israel's negotiating position in any eventual final settlement discussion, while simultaneously degrading Hamas's remaining operational space and governing capacity within an ever-shrinking strip. This is a strategy that trades international reputational cost — and there has been substantial reputational cost, reflected in the UN Security Council debates, European statements, and broader international legal scrutiny — for tangible territorial and security advantage, a trade Israel's current government has consistently calculated as worthwhile.

The Board of Peace's structural weakness deserves direct scrutiny, because it explains much of the implementation gap between the twenty-point plan's text and the reality on the ground. The Board of Peace and the Palestinian technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza were established and formally named in January 2026, but neither body has become operational on the ground in Gaza, leaving a governance vacuum that both Israeli military control and continued Hamas presence have filled by default. :antCitation[]{citations="e363b125-16c0-4376-b241-e6cf5b491f4f" injected="space"} A peace architecture that exists on paper but lacks operational presence on the ground cannot enforce the very ceasefire terms it was created to oversee, which is precisely the dynamic that has allowed violation counts to climb into the thousands without triggering any binding consequence for either party.

The American mediating role in this conflict carries an inherent asymmetry that distinguishes it from Washington's posture in, for instance, the Russia-Ukraine negotiations. The United States has continued large-scale arms transfers and diplomatic backing to Israel throughout this period, even while nominally overseeing a ceasefire Israel has violated thousands of times, a dynamic that international legal scholars have noted leaves the agreement functioning as a political instrument rather than a strongly enforceable legal one, given the absence of meaningful consequences for the violating party. :antCitation[]{citations="7e2ab87a-d81b-4a44-8f75-eb840c743cdd" injected="space"} This is not a minor technical asymmetry. It is the central reason the ceasefire has been able to persist nominally while failing functionally: the principal mediator and principal enforcer of the agreement is also the principal arms supplier and diplomatic protector of the party most frequently cited for violations.

Hamas's calculation through this period has rested on a parallel logic of attrition, betting that continued international attention on Gaza's humanitarian catastrophe, combined with growing fatigue in Washington and among European publics over the war's duration, will eventually force a settlement on terms more favorable than immediate disarmament. Israeli officials have characterized this as Hamas actively rebuilding its military and civilian capabilities and tightening its control over Gaza even while nominally party to the ceasefire, framing the group's posture as preparation for a future confrontation rather than genuine transition toward peace. :antCitation[]{citations="4f047c5f-5a5b-4e12-b69c-1c968fcf575f" injected="space"} Whether this assessment is accurate or itself serves Israel's own strategic interest in justifying continued territorial control is a genuinely contested question, and the available public evidence supports elements of both readings.

Global Impact

The conflict's prolongation has reshaped regional alignments in ways that will likely outlast whatever specific settlement eventually concludes the Gaza war. Arab and Gulf states that joined the Board of Peace framework, including Bahrain, Pakistan, and others among the roughly sixty countries invited to participate, have done so while simultaneously voicing sustained criticism of Israel's conduct of the war and its continued occupation posture, reflecting the genuine tension Arab governments face between formal participation in a US-led diplomatic architecture and domestic public opinion that remains intensely critical of Israeli actions in Gaza.

The League of Arab States has characterized Israel's posture as one of "permanent war," explicitly rejecting the notion that the ceasefire framework represents genuine progress toward Palestinian statehood, while also noting that Iran's attacks on Arab states during its confrontation with the US and Israel should not be allowed to divert attention from continued Israeli occupation of Palestinian and other Arab territories. :antCitation[]{citations="80dba41b-142a-4cbc-b540-42d68cdfcaf8" injected="space"} This dual criticism — of both Iran's regional disruption and Israel's occupation policies — illustrates how the broader Middle East's strategic landscape has become genuinely multipolar in its grievances, with Arab states increasingly unwilling to subordinate the Palestinian question to whatever other regional crisis happens to be dominating Washington's attention in a given month.

For Europe, the conflict's continuation has produced a familiar but increasingly strained pattern: declaratory statements supporting the ceasefire and the eventual goal of a two-state solution, paired with limited practical leverage over either Israeli or American policy. UN officials have specifically flagged Israel's approval of 34 new settlements across Area C and its continued withholding of nearly $2.5 billion in Palestinian clearance revenue as developments that, taken together, are undermining any realistic prospect of a two-state solution, regardless of how the Gaza ceasefire's implementation eventually proceeds.

:antCitation[]{citations="c3ce7d00-ac49-4f48-8915-14c89edda2a6" injected="space"}

For the broader Indo-Pacific and South Asian audience Global Chanakya serves, the Israel-Palestine conflict's trajectory matters as a case study in how great-power-brokered ceasefires function — or fail to function — when the mediating power maintains a fundamental military and diplomatic alignment with one party to the conflict. The pattern bears watching for its potential relevance to other protracted disputes where American mediation, however well-intentioned, operates from a position of structural asymmetry rather than genuine neutrality.

Risk Assessment

The most acute and immediate risk is a formal Israeli decision to resume full-scale combat operations in Gaza, explicitly threatened by Israeli security sources if Hamas continues refusing disarmament. Such a resumption would represent a return to the war's most destructive phase rather than its continuation at the current reduced but still lethal intensity, with correspondingly severe humanitarian consequences for a population that the UN and EU's joint Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment has already estimated requires $71.4 billion in reconstruction support over the next decade, support that would become substantially harder to mobilize and deliver amid renewed active combat.

A status quo should not be an option to anyone — Gaza's prolonged division leaves two million people without a viable future while entrenching a dangerous, unsustainable territorial fragmentation.

A second significant risk involves the Lebanon front's continued instability spilling into a broader Israel-Hezbollah confrontation independent of, but likely to interact with, Gaza's trajectory. The repeated cycle of ceasefire announcement and rejection between Israel and Hezbollah through April, May, and June 2026 demonstrates a level of agreement instability that exceeds even Gaza's troubled implementation record, and any serious deterioration on this front carries the added danger of drawing in Iran's continued, if currently ceasefire-constrained, regional posture following its own confrontation with the US and Israel earlier in the year.

A third risk lies in the West Bank's accelerating settlement expansion functioning as a slower-moving but ultimately more structurally consequential threat to any eventual two-state framework than Gaza's more visible violence. Settlement expansion of the scale approved in March 2026 progressively forecloses the territorial contiguity any genuine Palestinian state would require, meaning that even a hypothetical full resolution of the Gaza disarmament impasse would leave the broader Palestinian statehood question further from realistic achievement than it was before this settlement wave, independent of Gaza's specific trajectory.

A fourth risk involves the precedent this ceasefire's enforcement gap sets for international conflict resolution more broadly. A peace framework that can be violated more than three thousand times without triggering binding consequence for the violating party establishes a troubling template — one that other states observing this process, facing their own territorial disputes, may reasonably conclude demonstrates that international ceasefire architecture functions primarily as a tool for managing international perception rather than genuinely constraining the conduct of the more powerful party to any given conflict.

A fifth risk, more diffuse but corrosive over time, involves the humanitarian catastrophe's continued normalization. With acute food insecurity still affecting more than three-quarters of Gaza's population and the vast majority of children receiving no meaningful education, the territory risks producing a generation shaped overwhelmingly by displacement, deprivation, and unresolved trauma — conditions that historical precedent across multiple protracted conflicts suggests tend to entrench rather than dissolve the underlying drivers of future violence, regardless of whatever specific political settlement is eventually reached at the leadership level.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis — the following projections are analytical simulations grounded in current trends, not confirmed intelligence or guaranteed outcomes.

Scenario One: Continued Managed Low-Intensity Conflict (Most Likely, roughly 45% probability)

The current pattern persists through the remainder of 2026: a nominal ceasefire under near-constant violation, continued Israeli territorial consolidation within Gaza beyond the original yellow line, continued Hamas refusal to fully disarm, and a Board of Peace that remains largely non-operational on the ground. Humanitarian conditions remain severe but stabilize at current levels rather than deteriorating further or improving substantially. This scenario essentially extends the present equilibrium — neither full resolution nor full-scale renewed war — indefinitely.

Scenario Two: Formal Resumption of Full-Scale Gaza Combat (Moderate Likelihood, roughly 30% probability)

Israel formally declares the disarmament impasse unresolvable through continued negotiation and resumes large-scale military operations in Gaza, framed as completing the war's originally stated objectives. This would represent a return to the conflict's most destructive phase, with humanitarian consequences severe enough to likely trigger renewed, intensified international condemnation and potential strain on the Board of Peace framework's remaining international participants, even if it does not alter the underlying American diplomatic and material support for Israel's position.

Scenario Three: Negotiated Disarmament Breakthrough (Lower Likelihood, roughly 15% probability)

Sustained pressure from Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey, combined with a genuine American push to operationalize the Board of Peace and the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, produces a negotiated disarmament framework Hamas accepts in exchange for credible guarantees regarding Palestinian governance and eventual statehood prospects. This would represent the scenario most consistent with the twenty-point plan's original stated objectives, though it remains the least probable near-term outcome given the entrenched positions both parties have maintained throughout 2026.

Scenario Four: Lebanon Front Escalation Drawing Broader Regional Involvement (Lower-Moderate Likelihood, roughly 10% probability)

The repeated Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire cycle finally breaks down into sustained, large-scale conflict rather than the intermittent strikes and renegotiated truces characterizing the period through June 2026, potentially drawing renewed Iranian involvement despite its own ceasefire with the United States and complicating the broader regional diplomatic landscape that has, so far, kept the Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran fronts at least nominally separate from one another.

Intelligence Forecast

Watch closely for any formal Israeli announcement of renewed large-scale Gaza operations, particularly following any further breakdown in the already strained disarmament talks Mladenov has been conducting directly with Hamas representatives; a formal resumption announcement would represent the clearest signal of Scenario Two materializing. Watch the Board of Peace's operational status specifically — whether the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza and the Office of the High Representative for Gaza actually begin functioning on the ground rather than existing only as named but inactive institutions, since their continued non-operational status is the single clearest indicator of the broader peace plan's practical failure.

Watch West Bank settlement approval patterns closely through the remainder of 2026; further large-scale Area C approvals following March's record decision would represent continued, deliberate foreclosure of two-state territorial viability independent of Gaza's trajectory. Watch the Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire's durability beyond the June 19 truce; given the pattern of repeated breakdown and renegotiation already established, continued stability beyond several weeks would itself represent a meaningfully positive signal relative to the established baseline.

Watch humanitarian aid delivery figures against the ceasefire's stipulated targets as a leading indicator of broader implementation faith; continued, significant shortfalls below the agreed 600-truck daily target would suggest Israel's practical commitment to the ceasefire's humanitarian provisions remains limited regardless of its rhetorical positioning. Watch international legal proceedings and Security Council resolution implementation specifically tied to Resolution 2803, since formal international legal accountability mechanisms, however slow-moving, represent one of the few levers outside direct American-Israeli bilateral dynamics that could meaningfully alter incentive structures over a longer time horizon.

Final Strategic Takeaway

The Gaza ceasefire's first eight months have demonstrated something important and uncomfortable about how great-power-brokered peace processes function when the mediating power is also the principal military patron of one party to the conflict: such processes can stop the most visible, intense phase of violence while leaving almost every underlying structural driver of the conflict fully intact. Hostages came home. Some prisoners were released. The headline declaration of "war's end" generated exactly the political credit President Trump's administration sought to claim. And underneath that declaration, more than three thousand recorded violations, a death toll that has continued climbing by the hundreds, a territory progressively compressed and divided, and a disarmament impasse that no party has shown genuine willingness to resolve on terms the other side will accept.

The honest assessment of the Israel-Palestine conflict's trajectory in 2026 is that the war has not ended; it has been relabeled, with the underlying contest over Gaza's governance, the West Bank's territorial future, and the broader Palestinian statehood question every bit as unresolved as before October 2025, only now obscured behind a diplomatic architecture that exists more substantially on paper and in press releases than on the ground in Gaza itself. Until the Board of Peace becomes genuinely operational, until disarmament or some credible alternative security framework is actually implemented rather than merely demanded, and until settlement expansion in the West Bank stops foreclosing the territorial preconditions for any eventual Palestinian state, the most accurate map of this conflict's escalation risk is not a forecast of when the next crisis erupts. It is a recognition that the current crisis, structurally, never actually stopped.

seo.title: Iran-Israel Proxy War Explained: 2026 Direct War Analysis
seo.description: Full breakdown of the Iran-Israel proxy war's collapse into direct conflict in 2026 — Operation Epic Fury, Hezbollah, Hormuz, and what comes next.

title: Iran-Israel Proxy War Explained: From Shadow War to Open War
excerpt: What began as a decades-long shadow war fought through Hezbollah, Hamas, and the Houthis erupted in February 2026 into direct US-Israeli strikes that killed Iran's Supreme Leader. This report explains how the proxy network built and broke.
content:
Iran-Israel Proxy War Explained: From Shadow War to Open War

For nearly four decades, Iran and Israel fought a war neither country officially declared. It was waged through intermediaries — Hezbollah rockets fired from southern Lebanon, Hamas tunnels dug beneath Gaza, Houthi missiles launched at Red Sea shipping, militia attacks on American bases in Iraq and Syria — a careful architecture of deniability that allowed Tehran to bleed Israel and its allies without ever putting the Islamic Republic's own territory or leadership directly in the crosshairs. That architecture, built across the careers of multiple Iranian supreme leaders and sustained through billions of dollars in funding, weapons transfers, and training programs across what Tehran called its "Axis of Resistance," collapsed entirely on the morning of February 28, 2026.

At 06:45 UTC that day, Israeli warplanes struck a residential compound in Tehran where Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was meeting with senior officials. He died in the strike, along with members of his family and several of his most senior commanders. Within minutes, American B-2 bombers and Tomahawk-armed warships joined the assault, targeting Iran's fortified ballistic missile facilities under an operation Washington called Epic Fury and Israel called Roaring Lion. The proxy war was over. What replaced it was the most direct, most destructive confrontation between Iran, Israel, and the United States in the Islamic Republic's history — a war that, even after a ceasefire and a formal memorandum of understanding, has left every element of the old proxy architecture either shattered, mutating, or fighting on regardless of what any document in Switzerland says.

Executive Summary

The Iran-Israel confrontation has undergone a fundamental transformation over the past eighteen months, evolving from a decades-old proxy war fought primarily through non-state armed groups into direct state-on-state warfare. The June 2025 "Twelve-Day War" — in which Israel struck Iranian nuclear and military facilities, killing senior commanders and scientists, with the United States joining to strike three nuclear sites before a ceasefire took hold — proved to be only the opening act. Mass anti-government protests inside Iran in early 2026, combined with sustained Israeli lobbying of President Trump, produced authorization for a far larger operation: Operation Epic Fury, launched February 28, 2026, which killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in its opening strikes and triggered more than five weeks of direct combat between Iran on one side and the United States and Israel on the other.

The war's costs have been staggering by any measure. The conflict produced the largest-ever supply disruption of the global oil market, with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and direct attacks on energy infrastructure rippling through natural gas, fertilizer, aviation, and tourism industries worldwide, while the cost to the US military alone was estimated at nearly $29 billion by mid-May, with the Pentagon requesting a further $200 billion, and Iran assessing damage to its own economy at between $300 billion and as much as $1 trillion. :antCitation[]{citations="f76cdb25-e1bf-4681-b37a-758c16548396" injected="space"} A ceasefire was reached on April 7-8, but proved immediately fragile, with Israel launching a major bombing campaign against Hezbollah in Lebanon mere hours after the announcement, an act Iran characterized as a direct violation given its insistence that any ceasefire encompass the Lebanon front as well.

What followed was nearly three months of brinkmanship centered on the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes, with the United States imposing a naval blockade on Iranian shipping while Iran maintained its own blockade of the waterway, producing what observers described as a "dual blockade" of the Persian Gulf. A formal Memorandum of Understanding was digitally signed on June 15, 2026, by President Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, extending the ceasefire by sixty days, authorizing toll-free reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, lifting the US naval blockade, and initiating sixty days of nuclear negotiations, with a formal signing ceremony scheduled for June 19 in Switzerland. :antCitation[]{citations="3c6b6ac7-5967-4194-aa50-66c07d72dbd2" injected="space"} Even as this diplomatic process unfolded, however, Israeli strikes on Lebanon continued, and the proxy network's most resilient node — Hezbollah — has shown no sign of standing down regardless of what Tehran and Washington agree to on paper.

This report traces the proxy war's original architecture, explains how each node of Iran's regional network functioned and how each has fared through the direct war's eruption, and assesses what remains of Tehran's "Axis of Resistance" as the region moves into an uncertain post-war phase that, by every available account, has not actually ended the underlying conflict so much as changed its form once again.

Background

Iran's proxy strategy emerged from a specific strategic logic developed after the 1979 Islamic Revolution: a militarily and economically constrained Iran, isolated by Western sanctions and lacking the conventional military capacity to confront Israel or the United States directly, could nonetheless project power and impose costs on its adversaries by cultivating, arming, and funding non-state armed groups across the region that shared Tehran's broader ideological hostility to Israel and American regional influence. This network became known, in Iranian state messaging, as the Axis of Resistance, and it was built methodically over four decades.

Hezbollah, founded in Lebanon in the early 1980s with direct Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps support, became the network's flagship asset — a heavily armed, politically entrenched force controlling substantial territory in southern Lebanon and wielding genuine influence within Lebanon's formal government structures. Hamas, an originally distinct Palestinian Islamist movement with roots in the Muslim Brotherhood, developed a increasingly close, though historically more transactional, relationship with Tehran over time, receiving funding, weapons technology, and training even as the two maintained different ideological foundations — Hamas Sunni, Iran's leadership Shia. The Houthi movement in Yemen, which seized control of large portions of the country including the capital Sanaa during Yemen's civil war, became another increasingly important node, particularly for its demonstrated willingness to strike shipping in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Various Iraqi and Syrian militias, operating under the broad umbrella of "Popular Mobilization Forces" and similar designations, rounded out the network, providing Tehran with strike capability against American forces stationed across Iraq and Syria.

This proxy architecture allowed Iran to wage what amounted to sustained warfare against Israeli and American interests while maintaining a degree of plausible deniability and avoiding direct retaliation against Iranian territory for years at a stretch. The system's logic depended on Israel and the United States calculating that retaliation against the proxies themselves, while costly and recurring, was preferable to direct strikes on Iran that risked a far larger regional conflagration. That calculation held, with periodic exceptions, for decades.

The system's first major rupture came with the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel and the subsequent Gaza war, which set off a cascading sequence of escalation across every node of Iran's network simultaneously. Hezbollah opened a sustained front against northern Israel in solidarity with Hamas. The Houthis began attacking Red Sea shipping linked to Israel. Iraqi militias intensified strikes on American bases. Israel responded with an increasingly aggressive campaign against the network's leadership and infrastructure, including the assassination of Hamas political leader Ismail Haniyeh and a strike on the Iranian consulate in Damascus, both of which prompted direct Iranian missile strikes on Israeli territory in April and October 2024 — the first time in decades Iran had struck Israel directly rather than exclusively through proxies.

The proxy war's logic finally broke down completely with the Twelve-Day War of June 2025. Israel bombed military and nuclear facilities across Iran in a surprise attack lasting from June 13 to June 24, 2025, assassinating senior military leaders, nuclear scientists, and politicians while damaging or destroying Iranian air defenses, with Iran retaliating with over 550 ballistic missiles and more than 1,000 suicide drones targeting Israeli population centers and military, energy, and government sites, before the United States intercepted Iranian attacks and itself bombed three Iranian nuclear facilities on June 22. :antCitation[]{citations="16d81c61-5e7a-40bc-8394-417290b9adb3" injected="space"} A ceasefire took hold on June 24, but it proved to be merely an intermission rather than a conclusion.

Current Situation

The interlude between the Twelve-Day War and the far larger conflict that followed lasted barely eight months, and it was Iran's own internal political fragility, as much as any external trigger, that set the stage for what came next. At the beginning of 2026, Iran experienced its most widespread domestic demonstrations in decades, which the government suppressed with significant violence, even as Israel's security cabinet authorized additional strikes codenamed Operation Iron Strike in early January, with officials calculating that further strikes, or even the credible threat of them, would compound the political destabilization Iran's leadership was already facing from the street protests.

:antCitation[]{citations="4664116c-b75d-44d4-8b56-b95c5ea8a665" injected="space"}

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu used this moment of Iranian vulnerability to press President Trump directly for a far more ambitious joint operation than the Twelve-Day War had attempted — one explicitly targeting Iran's top leadership rather than solely its military and nuclear infrastructure. Following high-level meetings in February 2026, Trump authorized Operation Epic Fury, with reports indicating that Israeli intelligence provided by Netanyahu was a decisive factor in the decision to proceed. :antCitation[]{citations="7bbd0c79-98a2-403f-bcf4-e5ee4c31be3d" injected="space"} The operation's scale and ambition exceeded anything in the prior conflict by an order of magnitude. At 06:35 UTC on February 28, Trump gave the order to proceed, and ten minutes later CENTCOM announced strikes against Iran using Tomahawk missiles, HIMARS launchers, and long-range standoff weapons, while the Israeli Air Force simultaneously launched an unprecedented wave of decapitation strikes that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei along with several senior officials and members of his family who were attending meetings at his residential compound.

:antCitation[]{citations="caf4dc87-70e0-4e37-bacc-553a3228dc9d" injected="space"}

Iran's retaliation was immediate and expansive, targeting not just Israel but the broader American regional security architecture and Gulf shipping infrastructure. The IRGC announced the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to US- and Israel-allied shipping within hours of the initial strikes, triggering a global oil-price spike that would shadow the remainder of the conflict, while Iran retaliated within hours with hundreds of drones and ballistic missiles. :antCitation[]{citations="43f316c6-1e50-4fe4-9073-b3ac4e71972f" injected="space"} Iran also retaliated by firing missiles at seven Gulf states, hitting civilian infrastructure and airports in the United Arab Emirates, residential areas in Qatar, and an apartment building in Bahrain, demonstrating the conflict's rapid spillover well beyond the Iran-Israel bilateral dimension.

:antCitation[]{citations="08f06fd0-8d88-424c-8193-13cada2faed1" injected="space"}

Leadership succession inside Iran proceeded with remarkable speed despite the decapitation strike's apparent intent to produce paralysis. The Iranian regime replaced Ali Khamenei with his son, Mojtaba Khamenei, even as the broader military and political system continued struggling under sustained attack, with the Revolutionary Guard Corps publicly declaring readiness for complete obedience to the new supreme leader within days of the transition. :antCitation[]{citations="1562ac04-f050-49c7-b983-4fe3f90b2a9d" injected="space"} This succession, while accomplished without the total institutional collapse some American and Israeli planners may have hoped to trigger, nonetheless represents a significant and still poorly understood shift in the Islamic Republic's internal power structure, given Mojtaba Khamenei's far thinner public political record compared to his father.

The war's most consequential and economically disruptive front proved to be the Strait of Hormuz rather than any single battlefield engagement. By late March, IRGC officials suggested Iran might push its Houthi allies in Yemen to block the Bab el-Mandeb Strait as well, further straining global shipping, and on March 28 the Houthis did launch missiles and drones toward Israel, opening yet another front in the expanding regional conflict despite having reached their own separate ceasefire with the United States the previous year regarding Red Sea shipping attacks. :antCitation[]{citations="c78d5e38-951b-4e12-a661-d5cfa78933fe" injected="space"} The danger of crossfire and Iranian threats led to severe disruption of traffic through the Strait, one of the world's most volatile oil chokepoints, producing fuel shortages across parts of Asia and rippling effects through the global economy.

:antCitation[]{citations="e8b8fd1c-ac49-4009-88e4-7413a8b72161" injected="space"}

The first ceasefire, reached after more than five weeks of fighting, demonstrated almost immediately how unstable the broader regional architecture beneath it remained. Just hours after the United States and Iran announced their April 7-8 ceasefire, disagreement emerged over whether Lebanon was included in its scope, and the IDF conducted a blitz across Lebanon that killed hundreds of people and wounded more than 1,000 others, straining the fragile ceasefire between the United States and Iran even as it nominally held on the primary Iran-Israel front. :antCitation[]{citations="6626c6f7-9267-4058-877a-c28373f3a22b" injected="space"} Washington subsequently pressed Israel to de-escalate specifically on the Lebanon track, leading to direct Israel-Lebanon engagement and an eventual, though similarly fragile, separate ceasefire arrangement.

The months that followed settled into a pattern of mutual economic strangulation centered on the Strait of Hormuz, with neither side willing to fully back down. After Iran refused to reopen the Strait, blaming continued Israeli attacks on Lebanon, and following the failure of Pakistan-brokered talks in Islamabad, Trump announced a US naval blockade of Iran beginning April 13, producing what observers termed a "dual blockade" of the Persian Gulf — Iran blocking the strait from one direction, the United States blockading Iranian ports from the other. :antCitation[]{citations="50e3789c-93cb-487f-a9d6-0d767a89d3e4" injected="space"} Trump's public diplomatic posture through this period proved notably unreliable as a guide to actual progress. Trump falsely claimed more than thirty times since March that the United States and Iran were nearing a deal to end the war, with no resolution occurring after each claim, before later admitting he had been deliberately manipulating financial markets upward by continuously emphasizing the possibility of a peace deal, citing his own fear of broader economic catastrophe as the reason he eventually committed to a genuine settlement.

:antCitation[]{citations="272f2315-bae1-41d8-99d5-5047117ae491" injected="space"}

The eventual diplomatic resolution, brokered substantially by Pakistan with support from Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey, produced the Islamabad Memorandum framework that culminated in the formal Memorandum of Understanding signed June 15. Even as this agreement formally extended the ceasefire and addressed the Hormuz blockade, Israel continued strikes across southern Lebanon as of June 17, despite the MOU's stated requirement to end hostilities "on all fronts," with Lebanon's Ministry of Health reporting a cumulative toll that had risen to 3,826 killed and 11,851 wounded by that point. :antCitation[]{citations="0118a345-50bd-46b6-9b42-b3af465e6dd8" injected="space"} Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi stated bluntly that without the withdrawal of Israeli forces from territories they occupied, the war could not be considered fully concluded — a direct signal that Tehran views the Lebanon front's continuation as an unresolved breach of the broader settlement, regardless of the bilateral US-Iran progress.

:antCitation[]{citations="bd99d9d8-dc00-4125-af14-c6bf777dec3e" injected="space"}

Strategic Analysis

The shift from proxy war to direct war represents one of the most significant strategic ruptures in Middle Eastern security architecture in decades, and understanding why it happened requires recognizing what changed in the underlying calculus on both sides. For Israel, the cumulative effect of October 7, 2023, and the subsequent multi-front war against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iranian-backed militias appears to have produced a decisive shift in threat tolerance: rather than continuing to absorb periodic proxy attacks while degrading the network incrementally, Israeli leadership concluded that only direct, decapitating strikes against Iran's own leadership and nuclear infrastructure could durably resolve the threat the network represented. This is a genuinely consequential doctrinal shift — from containment and attrition of proxies toward direct confrontation with the state sponsoring them.

For the United States, the decision to join Israel's strikes with direct American military force, including the assassination-enabling intelligence sharing and the use of strategic bombers against fortified Iranian facilities, represents a similarly significant departure from the post-Iraq War caution that had characterized American Iran policy for nearly two decades. Trump's framing of the operation's core objective — permanently eliminating Iran's nuclear weapons ambitions, following Tehran's apparent reconstitution of nuclear and missile programs after the Twelve-Day War's initial strikes — reflects a calculation that incremental strikes and sanctions pressure had definitively failed to achieve nonproliferation objectives, leaving direct, large-scale military action as the only remaining tool perceived to offer a durable solution.

Iran's domestic political fragility at the moment Epic Fury launched cannot be overstated as a contributing strategic factor. A regime already managing its most significant protest wave in decades, with internal tension reportedly extending into disagreements between President Masoud Pezeshkian and the IRGC's military leadership over conduct of the war, faced the additional shock of losing its supreme leader and much of its senior military command structure within the war's opening hours. Pezeshkian reportedly clashed directly with IRGC chief-commander Ahmad Vahidi over how the war was being conducted, warning that without a ceasefire, Iran's economy could collapse within three to four weeks — an extraordinarily candid acknowledgment of internal regime stress emerging even as the war was actively underway.

:antCitation[]{citations="9739ca48-2faa-44c6-a678-0bbe0096a05e" injected="space"}

The succession to Mojtaba Khamenei, accomplished with surprising institutional speed, suggests Iran's clerical and security establishment had at minimum contingency-planned for exactly this scenario, even if the specific timing caught them by surprise. What remains genuinely uncertain is whether the new supreme leader, lacking his father's decades of accumulated personal authority and ideological credibility within the system, can sustain the same degree of internal cohesion the Islamic Republic has relied upon throughout previous crises, particularly given the scale of damage Iran's conventional military and nuclear infrastructure has sustained.

The proxy network's own fate through this period reveals a critical asymmetry worth examining carefully. Hamas, already severely degraded by two years of war in Gaza prior to Epic Fury's launch, played essentially no independent operational role in the 2026 conflict, having already been pushed into the ceasefire and disarmament negotiations covered extensively elsewhere on this platform. The Houthis, by contrast, demonstrated continued operational relevance and willingness to escalate even while nominally bound by a separate ceasefire with Washington, suggesting Yemen's geography and the movement's distance from direct retaliatory reach gives it a persistent capacity for disruptive action that the network's other nodes have largely lost.

Hezbollah represents the network's most strategically significant remaining asset and the clearest illustration of why declaring the broader Iran-Israel conflict "over" based on the US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding alone is analytically premature. Netanyahu's continued public commitment to intensifying strikes in Lebanon even as the broader US-Iran diplomatic track progressed toward formal agreement, alongside hardline Israeli political figures pushing for even more maximalist objectives including cutting Lebanese electricity and reoccupying Beirut's southern suburbs, demonstrates that Israel's war aims regarding Hezbollah specifically have not been resolved by, and may not be fully subordinate to, the broader Iran settlement. :antCitation[]{citations="96213907-fad3-423b-9304-e3bdb340b062" injected="space"} This matters enormously: a settlement that ends direct Iran-Israel-US hostilities while leaving the Hezbollah-Israel front unresolved is not actually a comprehensive resolution of the underlying conflict, merely a narrowing of its most dangerous and economically disruptive dimension.

Global Impact

The 2026 Iran war's economic disruption has been genuinely unprecedented in scale for a single regional conflict. The Strait of Hormuz closure and subsequent dual blockade produced the largest-ever supply disruption of the global oil market, with cascading effects across natural gas, fertilizer, aviation, and tourism sectors and substantial volatility across global financial markets throughout the conflict's duration. :antCitation[]{citations="6cd7c374-c230-4a35-b9f1-975703af3b95" injected="space"} These effects reached well beyond the Middle East itself, contributing directly to the energy emergency the Philippines declared amid Strait of Hormuz disruptions, complicating the Russia-Ukraine peace process by consuming American diplomatic bandwidth, and feeding into broader global inflationary pressure that several major economies struggled to manage through the first half of 2026.

For the Gulf states, the war's spillover into their own territory and infrastructure represented a sobering demonstration of how quickly a bilateral Iran-Israel-US confrontation can become a genuinely multilateral regional crisis. Iranian missile strikes on civilian infrastructure and airports across the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Bahrain, alongside attacks on commercial vessels and continued threats against American partner nations, forced Gulf governments into the uncomfortable position of bearing substantial costs from a war they had no direct role in starting, with the cost to Arab countries alone estimated at $120 billion by the end of March.

:antCitation[]{citations="0f95a250-f14c-4e8b-b05c-ef83a16a5ad1" injected="space"}

For China, the war's disruption to global energy markets and shipping created both vulnerability and diplomatic opportunity. Xi Jinping's government pledged it would not provide military equipment to Iran while expressing interest in purchasing additional US oil to reduce its own dependence on Hormuz-transiting supplies, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent characterizing Chinese behind-the-scenes engagement on reopening the strait as very much in Beijing's own economic interest given China's substantial reliance on Gulf energy imports. :antCitation[]{citations="22a88d4d-edc6-4215-b0b0-b04ea1fc34cd" injected="space"} This careful, calculated Chinese posture — avoiding direct entanglement while quietly working to restore the energy flows its own economy depends upon — illustrates Beijing's broader strategic preference for benefiting from American overextension in Middle Eastern conflicts without bearing any of the direct costs or risks of involvement.

For India, the war's effects were felt directly and tragically. A US submarine sank the Iranian warship IRIS Dena off the coast of Galle, Sri Lanka, as it was returning from the International Fleet Review 2026 held in Visakhapatnam, India — an episode illustrating how thoroughly the conflict's reach extended into the broader Indian Ocean region and how Indian-hosted multilateral naval engagements became entangled, however incidentally, with the war's violence. :antCitation[]{citations="5d1f5df5-a79a-441b-9635-e65028579bbb" injected="space"} More broadly, India's continued energy import diversification efforts, balancing Gulf, Russian, and American supply sources, faced renewed pressure throughout the conflict's duration, reinforcing New Delhi's existing strategic emphasis on energy security diversification as a core national security priority.

For the broader international legal and diplomatic order, the war's conduct — including the deliberate targeting and killing of a sitting head of state in Khamenei, extensive civilian infrastructure damage across multiple Gulf states, and credible reports of internationally prohibited munitions use — has generated substantial legal and normative concern among international jurists and human rights organizations, even as the Trump administration has shown little inclination toward addressing these concerns through any formal accountability mechanism.

Risk Assessment

The most immediate and acute risk remains the Lebanon front's potential to reignite the broader conflict despite the formal US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding. Israel's demonstrated willingness to continue and even intensify Lebanon operations throughout the broader diplomatic process, combined with Hezbollah's continued operational capacity and explicit rejection of ceasefire terms it considers insufficient, means the single most volatile element of the entire Axis of Resistance network remains essentially unresolved, with genuine potential to draw renewed Iranian engagement if Tehran calculates that continued Israeli action against Hezbollah constitutes a breach of the broader settlement's spirit, as Foreign Minister Araghchi has already suggested.

Without the withdrawal of Israeli forces from territories they occupied, the war cannot be considered fully concluded.

A second significant risk involves the durability of Iran's internal political stability under Mojtaba Khamenei's leadership. A succession accomplished under conditions of active war, following the loss of senior military leadership and amid pre-existing domestic protest movements, carries inherent fragility that could manifest in unpredictable ways — ranging from internal power struggles within the security establishment to renewed mass unrest exploiting the regime's demonstrated vulnerability, with consequences for regional stability that are genuinely difficult to forecast given the opacity of internal Iranian elite politics.

A third risk concerns the sixty-day nuclear negotiation window established under the Memorandum of Understanding. Given Iran's stated position that it is not currently discussing its nuclear program as part of the broader ceasefire negotiations, any failure to reach a substantive nuclear agreement within this window — covering verification, enrichment limits, and sanctions relief — risks reproducing the precise conditions that led to war in the first place, particularly if Iran's damaged but not eliminated nuclear infrastructure proves capable of reconstitution, as occurred following the Twelve-Day War's initial strikes in 2025.

A fourth risk involves the Strait of Hormuz's continued vulnerability even after the formal blockade's lifting. With 327 vessels still anchored or stopped near Hormuz approaches as of mid-June and shipping experts projecting three to four months before traffic fully normalizes, the global energy market's recovery from this disruption remains incomplete, and any renewed flare-up — on the Lebanon front, around continued Houthi activity, or through a breakdown in the nuclear negotiation track — could rapidly reproduce the supply disruption that defined the war's most economically damaging phase.

:antCitation[]{citations="2a65a868-93d9-4b29-b2d8-1f2f7ecedd1a" injected="space"}

A fifth risk, more diffuse but strategically significant, involves the broader regional precedent this war has set regarding the threshold for direct state-on-state conflict in the Middle East. The successful, if extraordinarily costly, use of direct decapitation strikes against a nuclear-armed-adjacent state's top leadership establishes a template that other regional and global actors will study closely, with implications for crisis stability in other protracted state rivalries that extend well beyond the immediate Iran-Israel-US triangle.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis — the following projections are analytical simulations grounded in current trajectories, not confirmed intelligence or guaranteed outcomes.

Scenario One: Fragile Multi-Track Stabilization (Most Likely, roughly 40% probability)

The US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding holds at the bilateral level, the Strait of Hormuz fully reopens over the following several months, and nuclear negotiations proceed without producing a comprehensive deal but also without a renewed direct US-Iran confrontation. The Lebanon front remains separately, persistently volatile, with continued Israeli strikes and periodic Hezbollah responses that fall short of triggering a full reignition of the broader regional war, effectively settling into its own distinct, lower-intensity but unresolved confrontation parallel to the broader Iran-US-Israel stabilization.

Scenario Two: Nuclear Negotiation Failure and Renewed Direct Confrontation (Moderate Likelihood, roughly 25% probability)

The sixty-day nuclear negotiation window expires without a substantive agreement, with Iran refusing the verification and enrichment limits the United States demands, given the new leadership's need to demonstrate sufficient resolve domestically following the loss of Ali Khamenei. This produces renewed direct strikes, potentially on a smaller scale than the initial Epic Fury operation but still involving direct US or Israeli military action against remaining Iranian nuclear and military infrastructure.

Scenario Three: Lebanon Front Reignition Drawing Renewed Iranian Involvement (Moderate Likelihood, roughly 25% probability)

Continued Israeli operations against Hezbollah, potentially including the more maximalist objectives some Israeli political figures have publicly advocated, produce a scale of Lebanese civilian and Hezbollah casualties severe enough that Iran's leadership, despite its own severely degraded military capacity, calculates it must respond in some form to maintain credibility within what remains of the Axis of Resistance network, risking a renewed, though likely more limited, direct confrontation distinct from the broader nuclear negotiation track.

Scenario Four: Genuine Regional De-escalation and Diplomatic Normalization (Lower Likelihood, roughly 10% probability)

Iran's new leadership, recognizing the scale of damage sustained and the genuine economic catastrophe risk its own officials have acknowledged, pursues a more fundamental strategic reorientation away from proxy warfare and toward genuine diplomatic engagement, potentially including indirect normalization steps with Israel facilitated by Gulf and Pakistani mediation, paired with a substantive, verifiable nuclear agreement. This would represent the most favorable plausible outcome but requires a degree of Iranian strategic reorientation that current evidence does not yet strongly support.

Intelligence Forecast

Watch the Lebanon front closely as the single most likely trigger for renewed broader escalation; any significant intensification of Israeli operations beyond the current pattern, or any Hezbollah action that produces substantial Israeli civilian casualties, would represent the clearest leading indicator of Scenario Three materializing. Watch the nuclear negotiation track's substantive progress over its sixty-day window specifically regarding verification mechanisms and enrichment limits, since Iran's explicit current position of declining to discuss its nuclear program signals a genuine risk that this track could collapse entirely once the broader ceasefire-related negotiations conclude.

Watch Mojtaba Khamenei's consolidation of authority within Iran's security and clerical establishment over the coming months; any visible internal friction, factional struggle, or renewed mass protest activity would represent a significant indicator of continued regime fragility with unpredictable implications for Iran's external posture. Watch Strait of Hormuz shipping normalization data closely as a leading economic indicator; continued anchored-vessel backlogs beyond the projected three-to-four-month normalization window would suggest underlying confidence in the ceasefire's durability remains limited within the commercial shipping and insurance sectors specifically.

Watch Houthi activity in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb corridor independently of the broader Iran-US track, given the movement's demonstrated willingness to act with a degree of operational independence from Tehran's own ceasefire commitments. Watch Gulf state diplomatic and economic positioning, particularly regarding any further compensation claims or security guarantee requests directed at Washington given the substantial, largely uncompensated costs Gulf states absorbed from a war fought primarily by other parties on their doorstep.

Final Strategic Takeaway

The four-decade Iran-Israel proxy war did not end in 2026 so much as it was overtaken by something more dangerous: a direct war that proved both sides' old assumptions about the limits of acceptable escalation had quietly expired. Israel and the United States demonstrated a willingness to strike a sitting supreme leader directly, something that would have seemed almost unthinkable in prior decades of careful, proxy-mediated confrontation. Iran demonstrated, in turn, that even after losing its top leadership and absorbing catastrophic damage to its military and nuclear infrastructure, its state apparatus could reconstitute leadership and continue fighting for months rather than collapsing outright, a resilience that should recalibrate Western assumptions about regime fragility in Tehran going forward.

What remains of the old proxy network — a battered Hamas, a Hezbollah still fighting on Lebanon's ground despite every ceasefire announcement, Houthis still launching missiles, Iraqi militias still simmering — suggests the underlying architecture of Iranian regional influence has been damaged but not dismantled, and that the Memorandum of Understanding signed in Switzerland addresses the war's most economically disruptive symptom, the Strait of Hormuz, far more comprehensively than it addresses the war's actual root cause: a multi-decade contest for regional dominance between Iran and Israel that has now survived direct decapitation strikes, the death of a supreme leader, and global economic disruption on a scale rarely seen in a single regional conflict. The proxy war, in its old form, is finished. Whatever replaces it — a genuinely stabilized region, or merely a pause before the next escalation, this time potentially without the deniability the old proxy architecture once provided — remains the single most consequential open question in Middle Eastern geopolitics heading into the second half of 2026.
